target: Dr. Ruiz is a resident, and she writes a SOAP note after she sees a patient.
First, she writes the Subjective: the patient is a 45-year-old female with a 3-day history of productive cough and fever.
Then she adds the Objective: temperature 38.5, and rhonchi in the left lower lobe.
After that, she writes the Assessment: community-acquired pneumonia.
Next, she writes the Plan: azithromycin, chest X-ray, and follow-up in 5 days.
The attending reads the note and asks: What is your differential diagnosis?
Dr. Ruiz says: Please let me explain my assessment and plan.
She presents the note clearly, and the attending says it is complete.

Después escribe la Evaluación: neumonía adquirida en la comunidad.
Luego escribe el Plan: azitromicina, radiografía de tórax y seguimiento en 5 días.
El médico adjunto lee la nota y pregunta: ¿Cuál es su diagnóstico diferencial?
La Dra. Ruiz dice: Permítame explicar mi evaluación y plan.

passage.title: Practicing a Board Question
target: Ana is a foreign medical graduate, and she practices board questions with her friend Luis.
First, she reads the question stem: A 62-year-old man with hypertension presents with sudden crushing chest pain.
The stem says he is diaphoretic, and his blood pressure is 90/60.
Luis asks: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Ana checks the vital signs and the risk factors, then she looks at the answer choices.
She says: I think the answer is STEMI.
Then Luis asks: What is the first step in management?
Ana answers: The first step is a 12-lead EKG.

target: Dr. Lopez, a resident, is orienting a new foreign medical graduate today.

passage.title: Psychiatry Consult on the Ward
target: Dr. Ruiz is a resident, and she sees a new patient for a psychiatry consult.
The chief complaint is low energy and poor sleep for a month.
She says: I'd like to ask you some routine questions, and I ask everyone.
In the past two weeks, have you felt hopeless or had suicidal ideation?
The patient looks sad, and his affect is flat during the interview.
The resident checks for psychosis and asks if he hears voices.
He says no, and he understands that he is sick, so his insight is good.
She suspects a mood disorder, but she tells the attending that the diagnosis is not final.
They agree to start a safety plan and ask the team to watch him closely.

passage.title: Evidence on Morning Rounds
target: On morning rounds, Dr. Ruiz presents a patient with first-episode atrial fibrillation.
The attending asks: What is your recommendation, and why?
Dr. Ruiz says: I was unsure about the treatment, so I consulted UpToDate and cross-referenced the most recent guidelines.
She also read a systematic review and a randomized controlled trial.
Then she discusses the risks and benefits with the patient, because the patient's values matter.
The attending asks: How strong is the evidence for this?
She answers that evidence-based medicine combines the best available evidence, clinical experience, and the patient's values.
The attending says: Good, because evidence-based medicine is about knowing where to find the best evidence.

Luego habla con el paciente sobre los riesgos y beneficios, porque los valores del paciente importan.
El médico adscrito pregunta: ¿Qué tan sólida es la evidencia para esto?
Ella responde que la medicina basada en la evidencia combina la mejor evidencia disponible, la experiencia clínica y los valores del paciente.
El médico adscrito dice: Muy bien, porque la medicina basada en la evidencia consiste en saber dónde encontrar la mejor evidencia.

passage.title: Laceration Repair in the ED
target: Dr. Ruiz is a resident in the emergency department, and she is about to repair a hand laceration.

She tells the patient: I need you to hold very still, because I'm going to use local anesthetic.
You'll feel a small sting and then some pressure.
Tell me if you feel any pain beyond that.
The attending watches and says: Please check the gauze and the suture before we start.
Dr. Ruiz asks the nurse for a retractor, because she wants a better view of the wound.
After she finishes the wound closure, she explains the aftercare to the patient.

passage.title: Explaining a C-section Decision
target: Mrs. Rivera is in labor, and Dr. Patel, the resident, reviews her gestational age and her prenatal visit notes.
She asks: Are you having contractions?
After several hours, the cervix is not opening as expected, and the fetal heart tracing is not reassuring.
Dr. Patel talks with the attending, and they recommend a C-section.
She tells the patient: Based on the fetal heart tracing and your labor progress, the safest option for you and your baby is a C-section.
Then she says: I know this isn't what you planned.
She continues: Let me explain what happens next.
The team asks for informed consent first, and after surgery the nurse reviews postpartum care and incision care.
Dr. Patel asks: Do you have any questions?

passage.title: New Heart Failure on Rounds
target: On morning rounds, the resident presents a 70-year-old man to the attending.
The chief complaint is shortness of breath for 2 weeks, with leg swelling.
The EKG shows no acute changes, but the BNP is high.
The echocardiogram report says the ejection fraction is 30%.
The resident says: I'd start with an ACE inhibitor, a beta-blocker, and a loop diuretic.
I'd optimize the doses before discharge, because the patient needs close monitoring.
The attending asks about disposition, and the resident answers: I'd arrange cardiology follow-up within 2 weeks.
The attending agrees and asks the resident to write the plan.

passage.title: Ethics Discussion on Rounds
target: During rounds, the attending asks us to discuss an ethics case about Mr. Lopez.
He is confused, and the resident says he may lack capacity.
I explain: When a patient lacks capacity, I look for an advance directive first.
If there is none, I identify the legally recognized surrogate decision maker, usually the next of kin.
His daughter says he has a DNR order in his chart, but I want to verify it first.
The intern asks if we still need informed consent for a new procedure.
I answer that we need it from the surrogate, because the patient cannot decide now.
The goal is always to honor what the patient would have wanted.

passage.title: Thank-You Email After Interview
target: Maria is a foreign medical graduate, and she finished her residency interview yesterday.
This morning she sits down to write a thank-you email to the program director.
She writes: Dear Dr. Williams, thank you for taking the time to speak with me yesterday.
She wants to reinforce her interest, so she adds that the program is her top choice.
She also mentions one specific thing they discussed: the program's commitment to underserved communities.
She explains that this aligns with her long-term goals, because she wants to work in community clinics.
She closes the email with: I would be honored to train with your team.
Before she clicks send, she checks the spelling of the director's name and signs with Sincerely, Maria.

passage.title: My Residency Program Interview
target: Today I have my interview with the program director at an internal medicine residency program.
First, I introduce myself and explain why I chose this specialty.
Then the director gives me a clinical case, and the chief complaint is chest pain.
I say: Let me explain my reasoning, and I give a short differential diagnosis.
In the ethics scenario, a patient refuses treatment, so I check informed consent and ask the attending for help.
Next, I describe my research project and what I learned about teamwork.
At the end, I ask: Could you tell me more about mentorship in the program?
I close: Thank you for this conversation, and I hope to join your team.
